prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "JOHNSON & JOHNSON" (ticker JNJ). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)

   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)

   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?

   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?

summaries.gardner: J&J is a 140-year-old incumbent in a mature industry, so it does not fit Gardner's Rule Breaker profile of a top dog in an emerging industry. It does show some of his traits: a strong 30% one-year share-price gain, a well-known brand and a sustainable advantage in patented medicines, but it is not commonly called overvalued and its industry is not emerging.
summaries.buffett: J&J fits many Buffett tenets: an understandable business, 64 consecutive years of dividend increases, high returns on capital (ROIC about 20%), strong free cash flow (about $22 billion trailing) and an AAA balance sheet. The weaker points are talc litigation and a price of about 29 times trailing earnings and 22 times forward, which leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the diversified franchise of patented medicines and devices, the conservative AAA balance sheet and a culture anchored in Our Credo. Inverting, the risks are patent cliffs (Stelara, later Darzalex), drug price regulation and litigation, none likely fatal but all real; at about 22 times forward earnings the price is fair rather than cheap.
summaries.lynch: J&J is a classic Lynch stalwart: a large, steady grower (sales from continuing operations up every year from $78.7 billion in 2021 to $94.2 billion in 2025) that can deliver 30-50% gains over a few years. With a PEG around 3 and almost no insider buying, it fails Lynch's cheapness tests, and it is widely followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: J&J scores well on Fisher's points for R&D ($14.7 billion in 2025), a strong sales organisation, new products replacing maturing ones (about 25% of 2025 sales from products launched in the last five years) and long-term management. Gross margins have drifted down from 70.3% (2021) to 67.9% (2025), and litigation has raised questions about candour.
summaries.graham: J&J meets Graham's defensive-investor tests for size, financial strength, an unbroken dividend record and earnings growth over ten years (diluted EPS $5.48 in 2015 vs $11.03 in 2025). It fails the price tests: about 29 times trailing earnings and 7 times book value, far above the 15x and 22.5 limits.
summaries.thiel: From Thiel's lens J&J is not a zero-to-one company: it has some near-monopoly drugs (Darzalex in myeloma) and strong distribution, but no single technology ten times better than rivals and no secret others overlook. Its durability comes from a constantly renewed portfolio rather than one dominant monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth, operating discipline and a reasonable price relative to growth. J&J has disciplined operations, accelerating sales growth (guided 7.4% for 2026) and strong free cash flow, but mid-single to high-single digit growth at 22 times forward earnings is not the kind of compounding at a discount he usually seeks, and it is not an AI beneficiary.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on accelerating earnings, rising estimates and catalysts. J&J's sales growth has accelerated and guidance was raised in October 2026, but adjusted EPS guidance ($11.05-11.15) is below January's $11.43-11.63 because of acquisition charges and the stock fell 5.7% on Q3 results, so the setup is mixed.
summaries.smith: J&J matches Terry Smith's 'good company' tests: high returns on capital, a 68% gross margin, strong cash conversion and resilient demand for healthcare, and Fundsmith has held it before. The question for Smith would be price, with a free-cash-flow yield near 3.7%, and the drag from litigation.
summaries.greenblatt: On Greenblatt's Magic Formula J&J has a high return on capital (ROIC about 20%), but its earnings yield is modest: operating income of about $27 billion on an enterprise value of about $627 billion is roughly 4.3% (EV/EBIT about 23). It would rank as a quality company but not a cheap one.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for an extraordinary business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. J&J has a strong business and solid managers, but much of its free cash flow is paid out as dividends (payout about 62%) or used for large acquisitions rather than reinvested organically at high rates, and litigation weighs on governance.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress at low prices with little downside. J&J is simple enough and its permanent-loss risk is low, but after a 30% one-year rise and with the talc settlement largely priced in, it is not a heads-I-win-tails-I-don't-lose-much bargain.
summaries.wood: J&J is not a Cathie Wood-style disruptive innovator: it is a large incumbent. It does touch ARK themes through cell therapy (Carvykti), bispecific antibodies and surgical robotics (Ottava, still in development), but these are a small part of a $94 billion business.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria favour simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and strong balance sheets, all of which J&J offers. The gaps are limited upside at about 22 times forward earnings, litigation and drug-pricing exposure, and the absence of an obvious activist catalyst.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model, where a company passes its cost savings back to customers, does not describe J&J, which uses patents to keep prices high. It is a durable, well-run franchise, but its advantage comes from intellectual property and scale rather than ever-falling prices.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge markets with new technology. J&J serves huge, painful problems (cancer, heart disease, surgery), but it is a mature incumbent rather than a start-up riding a technology wave, so his venture lens fits it poorly.

momentum.evidence: JNJ shares rose 30.4% over the 52 weeks to 13 October 2026 (to $248.61) versus a 20.4% total return for the S&P 500 (SPY), though they fell 5.7% on the Q3 2026 report.

g4.evidence: CEO Joaquin Duato has executed the Kenvue separation and the Abiomed, Shockwave and Intra-Cellular acquisitions, and partners include Genmab (Darzalex) and Legend Biotech (Carvykti), but there is no celebrated backer beyond broad institutional ownership.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it Buy (16 of 23 Buy or Strong Buy) with an average target of $278.64, about 12% above the price; it is seldom called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It sells prescription medicines (64% of 2025 sales) and medical devices (36%), a structure a careful generalist can understand, even if individual drug pipelines are technical.

b2.evidence: It has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years and continuing-operations sales grew every year from 2021 to 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management is rational with capital and keeps an AAA balance sheet, but the repeated attempts to resolve talc claims through subsidiary bankruptcies (rejected in 2023 and 2025) drew criticism over candour and governance.

b6.evidence: Its acquisitions (Abiomed $16.6 billion, Shockwave about $13 billion, Intra-Cellular about $14.6 billion) fit its chosen areas rather than empire-building, but they are large and similar to peers' deal-making.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 20% and ROE about 26% (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), with net debt of only about $28 billion against roughly $27 billion of annual operating income.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was about $19.7 billion in 2025 and $22.2 billion over the trailing twelve months, close to underlying adjusted earnings.

b10.evidence: Market value is about $599 billion after spinning off Kenvue, but large retained cash has gone to acquisitions such as Abiomed whose returns are still being proven, so value creation per retained dollar is solid rather than exceptional.

safety.evidence: At $248.61 the stock trades at about 29 times trailing and 22 times forward earnings and 7 times book value, near the analyst average target, so there is little margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 22 times forward earnings for a high-quality AAA-rated company growing sales about 7% a year is reasonable but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: With 2025 sales spread over oncology, immunology, neuroscience and four device franchises and an AAA balance sheet, few things could make it fail outright; patent cliffs, pricing laws and litigation would hurt rather than destroy it.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests about $14.7 billion a year in R&D and buys growth assets, but much of its cash goes to dividends (payout about 62%), and pharma R&D returns are uneven.

ly2.evidence: It is a textbook stalwart: a large, steady grower with a simple story of new drugs (Tremfya, Carvykti, Rybrevant) replacing Stelara while MedTech grows.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 29 and forward P/E about 22, well above its single-digit to low-double-digit expected earnings growth (PEG about 3).

runway.evidence: Management targets double-digit growth by 2030 with a pipeline of potential $5 billion products, but it is already a $100 billion-plus business, which limits how fast it can grow.

ly7.evidence: Insiders own about 0.04% with no notable open-market buying, and the share count rose about 0.5% over the past year.

ly8.evidence: J&J is one of the most widely followed healthcare stocks, covered by more than 20 analysts.

fi2.evidence: About 25% of 2025 sales came from products launched in the past five years, and Tremfya, Darzalex, Carvykti and Rybrevant are replacing Stelara's lost sales.

fi3.evidence: R&D has produced major drugs such as Darzalex ($14.35 billion in 2025 sales), Tremfya ($5.16 billion), Erleada ($3.57 billion) and Carvykti ($1.89 billion).

fi4.evidence: Its global commercial organisation has made Darzalex the leading myeloma drug and sells into hospitals and pharmacies in most countries, with 43% of 2025 sales outside the US.

longterm.evidence: It spends about 15% of sales on R&D and bought pipeline companies, while protecting a 64-year record of dividend increases and quarterly earnings guidance.

gr1.evidence: Sales were $94.2 billion in 2025 and market value is about $599 billion.

ni10.evidence: J&J reported positive net earnings in each of the last ten years, including $26.8 billion in 2025, despite large talc and tax charges in some years.

gr4.evidence: It has paid dividends for decades and raised them for 64 consecutive years; the current annual rate is $5.36 a share.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $5.48 in 2015 to $11.03 in 2025, more than doubling (helped by a 2025 talc reserve reversal).

gr6.evidence: The price of $248.61 is about 34 times average diluted EPS from continuing operations over 2023-2025 ($5.20, $5.79, $11.03), well above 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 28.8 times P/B of about 7.05 gives roughly 203, far above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Some drugs lead their classes, such as Darzalex and Carvykti, but none is ten times better than every alternative across the business.

timing.evidence: Growth is accelerating as new launches offset Stelara's patent loss, while drug pricing reform, tariffs and litigation are headwinds.

th3.evidence: Products like Darzalex started by dominating a small myeloma niche and expanded into earlier treatment lines, but the company overall is already large in big markets.

team.evidence: Management is experienced and steady (CEO Joaquin Duato, a 35-year J&J veteran), but not an exceptional founder-led team.

th5.evidence: Its global sales forces, hospital relationships and payer contracts let it launch medicines and devices worldwide quickly.

durable.evidence: Healthcare demand and its diversified portfolio should last decades, but each drug's position is temporary and devices face new technology such as pulsed-field ablation and robotics.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of focusing on medicines and medtech is shared by many large peers rather than being a unique insight.

trend.evidence: It benefits from ageing populations and growth in cancer and immune-disease treatment, but it is not a leading AI or cloud beneficiary.

dr1.evidence: Sales growth accelerated to 5.9% in Q3 2026 and sales guidance was raised to $101.0-101.4 billion, but adjusted EPS guidance fell from January's $11.43-11.63 to $11.05-11.15 on acquisition-related charges.

dr2.evidence: By 2027-2028 the Stelara drag should fade and talc could be settled, but these improvements are widely expected.

dr4.evidence: Healthcare demand is not very sensitive to the economy, but US drug-pricing policy and tariffs are adverse while rates matter little to an AAA-rated company.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include completing the $5.5 billion talc settlement, the planned DePuy Synthes orthopaedics separation, new approvals for Tremfya, Rybrevant and Icotrokinra, and the Ottava robot.

dr7.evidence: As a mature, moderately priced stalwart with litigation risk it suits a core holding more than a large concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 67.9% in 2025, high for a company with a large device business.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 3.7% (P/FCF about 27), reasonable for an AAA-rated company but not cheap for its growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 23, an earnings yield of only about 4.3% on enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: The Stelara patent loss and talc litigation were temporary setbacks now largely priced in after the 30% one-year rise.

pa4.evidence: Diversified revenue, AAA credit and strong cash flow make permanent loss unlikely, though overpaying could still mean weak returns.

wo1.evidence: It is developing the Ottava surgical robot and uses AI in drug discovery and its CARTO mapping, but it is not a leader in these platforms.

wo2.evidence: Its costs do not fall rapidly with volume in a way that unlocks large new demand; it relies on patented pricing.

wo3.evidence: It combines cell therapy, bispecific antibodies, radiopharmaceuticals and robotics, but mostly as separate franchises.

wo4.evidence: Its markets are large and growing in the mid-to-high single digits, not set to multiply several times in five years.

ac3.evidence: Demand is little affected by commodities or rates, but drug-pricing laws, tariffs, currencies (43% of sales outside the US) and litigation are significant outside forces.

ns1.evidence: It keeps premium prices on patented drugs rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: With a strong pipeline it should remain a top healthcare company in 10-20 years, but it is not clearly stronger than today given patent expiries and new competitors.

va2.evidence: Its products treat cancer, autoimmune disease, heart disease and mental illness and support surgery, all large and painful problems.
